headline: Count ways to decode one or two final digits
statement: Digits 1..26 represent A..Z. Return how many ways the digit string s can be split into valid codes. A code cannot begin with zero, so 06 is invalid while 10 is valid. The result fits a signed 32-bit integer.
constraints: s contains decimal digits, possibly leading zeros
intuition: Every valid decoding of a prefix ends in either a one-digit code or a two-digit code. These cases are disjoint. Their counts come from shorter prefixes, so counting never requires constructing all decoded strings.
approach: Set dp[0]=1: the empty prefix supplies one way to begin a decoding.
For each prefix length i, add dp[i-1] if its final digit is not zero.
Also add dp[i-2] if its final two digits form a number from 10 to 26.
Return the count for the entire string.
correctness: Partition decodings by the length of their last code. Removing that code leaves a valid decoding of the preceding prefix, and appending it reconstructs exactly one full decoding. The two code lengths never overlap, so summing the applicable shorter-prefix counts is exact. Induction from dp[0]=1 establishes all entries.
bruteForce: Recursively try one- and two-digit codes at every position without memoization. Repeated suffixes cause exponential work.

complexity.explanation: Each prefix performs two constant-size digit checks; the table makes all prefix counts inspectable.

pitfalls: A zero contributes no single-digit decoding.
Two-digit codes must be between 10 and 26, not merely <=26.
